actions.mechanism: H.R.29: expanding specified immigration detention and State enforcement litigation
actions.candidate_exact_action_meaning: H.R.29 would extend the federal mandatory-custody category to the following offenses: burglary, theft, larceny or shoplifting. The four listed property-offense terms take the meaning assigned by the jurisdiction where the acts occurred. The exact bill adds an INA 236(c) mandatory-custody category requiring inadmissibility under INA 212(a)(6)(A), (6)(C), or (7) together with a specified criminal predicate: being charged, arrested, convicted, admitting commission, or admitting acts constituting the essential elements. These inadmissibility categories concern presence without admission/parole or undesignated arrival, material immigration fraud/false citizenship claims, and specified entry-document defects, subject to their existing statutory qualifications. DHS must issue a detainer for a person meeting the new ground and, if the person is not otherwise detained by Federal, State or local officials, effectively and expeditiously take custody. The bill also gives a State attorney general or other authorized State officer standing, on alleged harm to the State or residents (including financial harm in excess of $100), to seek appropriate injunctive relief in district court over five specified federal matters: INA 235(b)(1)/(2) detention/removal requirements; INA 236 release, bond or parole decisions; the existing INA 243(d) visa-discontinuance requirement for countries denying or unreasonably delaying acceptance; violation of the existing INA 212(d)(5)(A) case-by-case urgent-humanitarian/significant-public-benefit parole limits; and INA 241(a)(2) detention during the removal period. Courts must advance and expedite these cases to the greatest practicable extent. INA 236(e) removes its express release/grant shield while leaving the other printed discretionary-judgment/detention/revocation/denial restrictions, and INA 242(f)(1) receives an exception for the printed listed actions, while its separate final-removal-order injunction standard remains. These review changes do not establish a general right to enjoin every immigration action. The parole clause changes its named administering actor to the Secretary of Homeland Security. The baseline removal period is generally 90 days with specified starting/extension conditions; the bill adds litigation standing over its detention requirement rather than creating that period. The pre-existing narrow witness/cooperator-protection release exception remains, redesignated as INA 236(c)(4).
actions.candidate_short_description: H.R.29: expanding specified immigration detention and State enforcement litigation
actions.candidate_compact_description: H.R.29 would expand mandatory immigration custody and DHS detainers for the specified inadmissibility/offense combination (burglary, theft, larceny or shoplifting), and add harm-conditioned State suits over specified detention, release, parole and visa duties.
candidate_shared_limitations: The four listed property-offense terms take the meaning assigned by the jurisdiction where the acts occurred.

The new custody ground requires both inadmissibility under INA 212(a)(6)(A), (6)(C), or (7) and a listed offense predicate. Arrest or charge can suffice for the offense predicate; conviction is not required. Existing inadmissibility exceptions and waiver routes are not repealed, including specified battered-person/false-citizenship exceptions and document/fraud waivers.

The pre-existing INA 236(c) witness/cooperator-protection release exception is redesignated rather than repealed: release requires the specified protection necessity, no danger and likely appearance. Ordinary bond or parole is not substituted for that narrow exception.

State litigation requires alleged harm to the State or residents, including financial harm in excess of $100. Relief is appropriate injunctive relief and expedited handling to the greatest practicable extent; a filed suit or favorable judgment is not inferred.

Case-by-case humanitarian/significant-public-benefit parole limits and the conditional visa-discontinuance duty for countries refusing or delaying acceptance already exist. The bill adds State enforcement standing and related review changes; it does not newly create those substantive baseline limits.

The visa-discontinuance duty arises after the statutory federal notification that a foreign country denies or unreasonably delays acceptance after a request. It covers immigrant visas, nonimmigrant visas, or both for the specified nationals/residents in that country, and lasts until the statutory acceptance notice. These conditions are retained, not newly imposed.

The existing INA 236(c)(1) when-released framework remains; the new DHS detainer clause separately requires expeditious custody when the person is not otherwise detained. No actual detention timing or individual outcome is inferred.

This is a whole-bill House passage choice. It does not establish separate component positions, guilt, actual detention/removal, a successful suit or enactment. The parallel House and Senate bills remain distinct proposal episodes; later enacted text does not replace either exact voting version.

choice_meanings.Yea: supported passage of H.R.29 with its specified custody/detainer expansion and State enforcement-standing provisions
choice_meanings.Nay: opposed passage of H.R.29 with those provisions; no preferred alternative is established

Apprehension and detention of aliens (a) Arrest, detention, and release On a warrant issued by the Attorney General, an alien may be arrested and detained pending a decision on whether the alien is to be removed from the United States. Except as provided in subsection (c) and pending such decision, the Attorney General— (1) may continue to detain the arrested alien; and (2) may release the alien on— (A) bond of at least $1,500 with security approved by, and containing conditions prescribed by, the Attorney General; or (B) conditional parole; but (3) may not provide the alien with work authorization (including an "employment authorized" endorsement or other appropriate work permit), unless the alien is lawfully admitted for permanent residence or otherwise would (without regard to removal proceedings) be provided such authorization. (b) Revocation of bond or parole The Attorney General at any time may revoke a bond or parole authorized under subsection (a), rearrest the alien under the original warrant, and detain the alien. (c) Detention of criminal aliens (1) Custody The Attorney General shall take into custody any alien who— (A) is inadmissible by reason of having committed any offense covered in section 1182(a)(2) of this title, (B) is deportable by reason of having committed any offense covered in section 1227(a)(2)(A)(ii), (A)(iii), (B), (C), or (D) of this title, (C) is deportable under section 1227(a)(2)(A)(i) of this title on the basis of an offense for which the alien has been sentence 1 to a term of imprisonment of at least 1 year, or (D) is inadmissible under section 1182(a)(3)(B) of this title or deportable under section 1227(a)(4)(B) of this title, when the alien is released, without regard to whether the alien is released on parole, supervised release, or probation, and without regard to whether the alien may be arrested or imprisoned again for the same offense. (2) Release The Attorney General may release an alien described in paragraph (1) only if the Attorney General decides pursuant to section 3521 of title 18 that release of the alien from custody is necessary to provide protection to a witness, a potential witness, a person cooperating with an investigation into major criminal activity, or an immediate family member or close associate of a witness, potential witness, or person cooperating with such an investigation, and the alien satisfies the Attorney General that the alien will not pose a danger to the safety of other persons or of property and is likely to appear for any scheduled proceeding. A decision relating to such release shall take place in accordance with a procedure that considers the severity of the offense committed by the alien. (d) Identification of criminal aliens (1) The Attorney General shall devise and implement a system— (A) to make available, daily (on a 24-hour basis), to Federal, State, and local authorities the investigative resources of the Service to determine whether individuals arrested by such authorities for aggravated felonies are aliens; (B) to designate and train officers and employees of the Service to serve as a liaison to Federal, State, and local law enforcement and correctional agencies and courts with respect to the arrest, conviction, and release of any alien charged with an aggravated felony; and (C) which uses computer resources to maintain a current record of aliens who have been convicted of an aggravated felony, and indicates those who have been removed. (2) The record under paragraph (1)(C) shall be made available— (A) to inspectors at ports of entry and to border patrol agents at sector headquarters for purposes of immediate identification of any alien who was previously ordered removed and is seeking to reenter the United States, and (B) to officials of the Department of State for use in its automated visa lookout system. (3) Upon the request of the governor or chief executive officer of any State, the Service shall provide assistance to State courts in the identification of aliens unlawfully present in the United States pending criminal prosecution. (e) Judicial review The Attorney General's discretionary judgment regarding the application of this section shall not be subject to review. No court may set aside any action or decision by the Attorney General under this section regarding the detention or release of any alien or the grant, revocation, or denial of bond or parole.

claim_source_map.passage: (b) Inspection of applicants for admission (1) Inspection of aliens arriving in the United States and certain other aliens who have not been admitted or paroled (A) Screening (i) In general If an immigration officer determines that an alien (other than an alien described in subparagraph (F)) who is arriving in the United States or is described in clause (iii) is inadmissible under section 1182(a)(6)(C) or 1182(a)(7) of this title, the officer shall order the alien removed from the United States without further hearing or review unless the alien indicates either an intention to apply for asylum under section 1158 of this title or a fear of persecution. Such designation shall be in the sole and unreviewable discretion of the Attorney General and may be modified at any time. (II) Aliens described An alien described in this clause is an alien who is not described in subparagraph (F), who has not been admitted or paroled into the United States, and who has not affirmatively shown, to the satisfaction of an immigration officer, that the alien has been physically present in the United States continuously for the 2-year period immediately prior to the date of the determination of inadmissibility under this subparagraph. (ii) Referral of certain aliens If the officer determines at the time of the interview that an alien has a credible fear of persecution (within the meaning of clause (v)), the alien shall be detained for further consideration of the application for asylum. (iii) Removal without further review if no credible fear of persecution (I) In general Subject to subclause (III), if the officer determines that an alien does not have a credible fear of persecution, the officer shall order the alien removed from the United States without further hearing or review. (II) Record of determination The officer shall prepare a written record of a determination under subclause (I). Such record shall include a summary of the material facts as stated by the applicant, such additional facts (if any) relied upon by the officer, and the officer's analysis of why, in the light of such facts, the alien has not established a credible fear of persecution. A copy of the officer's interview notes shall be attached to the written summary. (III) Review of determination The Attorney General shall provide by regulation and upon the alien's request for prompt review by an immigration judge of a determination under subclause (I) that the alien does not have a credible fear of persecution. Such review shall include an opportunity for the alien to be heard and questioned by the immigration judge, either in person or by telephonic or video connection. Review shall be concluded as expeditiously as possible, to the maximum extent practicable within 24 hours, but in no case later than 7 days after the date of the determination under subclause (I). (IV) Mandatory detention Any alien subject to the procedures under this clause shall be detained pending a final determination of credible fear of persecution and, if found not to have such a fear, until removed. (iv) Information about interviews The Attorney General shall provide information concerning the asylum interview described in this subparagraph to aliens who may be eligible. An alien who is eligible for such interview may consult with a person or persons of the alien's choosing prior to the interview or any review thereof, according to regulations prescribed by the Attorney General. Such consultation shall be at no expense to the Government and shall not unreasonably delay the process. (v) "Credible fear of persecution" defined For purposes of this subparagraph, the term "credible fear of persecution" means that there is a significant possibility, taking into account the credibility of the statements made by the alien in support of the alien's claim and such other facts as are known to the officer, that the alien could establish eligibility for asylum under section 1158 of this title. (C) Limitation on administrative review Except as provided in subparagraph (B)(iii)(III), a removal order entered in accordance with subparagraph (A)(i) or (B)(iii)(I) is not subject to administrative appeal, except that the Attorney General shall provide by regulation for prompt review of such an order under subparagraph (A)(i) against an alien who claims under oath, or as permitted under penalty of perjury under section 1746 of title 28, after having been warned of the penalties for falsely making such claim under such conditions, to have been lawfully admitted for permanent residence, to have been admitted as a ref ugee under section 1157 of this title, or to have been granted asylum under section 1158 of this title. (D) Limit on collateral attacks In any action brought against an alien under section 1325(a) of this title or section 1326 of this title, the court shall not have jurisdiction to hear any claim attacking the validity of an order of removal entered under subparagraph (A)(i) or (B)(iii). (E) "Asylum officer" defined As used in this paragraph, the term "asylum officer" means an immigration officer who— (i) has had professional training in country conditions, asylum law, and interview techniques comparable to that provided to full-time adjudicators of applications under section 1158 of this title, and (ii) is supervised by an officer who meets the condition described in clause (i) and has had substantial experience adjudicating asylum applications. (F) Exception Subparagraph (A) shall not apply to an alien who is a native or citizen of a country in the Western Hemisphere with whose government the United States does not have full diplomatic relations and who arrives by aircraft at a port of entry. (G) Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands Nothing in this subsection shall be construed to authorize or require any person described in section 1158(e) of this title to be permitted to apply for asylum under section 1158 of this title at any time before January 1, 2014. (2) Inspection of other aliens (A) In general Subject to subparagraphs (B) and (C), in the case of an alien who is an applicant for admission, if the examining immigration officer determines that an alien seeking admission is not clearly and beyond a doubt entitled to be admitted, the alien shall be detained for a proceeding under section 1229a of this title. (B) Exception Subparagraph (A) shall not apply to an alien— (i) who is a crewman, (ii) to whom paragraph (1) applies, or (iii) who is a stowaway. (C) Treatment of aliens arriving from contiguous territory In the case of an alien described in subparagraph (A) who is arriving on land (whether or not at a designated port of arrival) from a foreign territory contiguous to the United States, the Attorney General may return the alien to that territory pending a proceeding under section 1229a of this title.

actions.candidate_exact_action_meaning: The exact House-passed H.R.23 requires the President, not later than 60 days after enactment and on an ongoing basis, to impose sanctions if the ICC is attempting to investigate, arrest, detain or prosecute a protected person. Covered foreign persons are those the President determines directly engage in or aid such an effort; materially assist, sponsor or provide specified support/goods/services for it; or are owned/controlled by, or currently act or purport to have acted for, a person directly engaging in it. For covered aliens, the bill makes them inadmissible, ineligible for visas or other entry documents, admission or parole, and any other INA benefit. Their visas/entry documents must be revoked regardless of issuance date, effective immediately and automatically canceling other valid visas/entry documents in their possession. The immigration sanctions also apply to each sanctioned foreign person's spouse, parent, sibling or adult child; the separate property-blocking requirement applies to the principal foreign persons described in 3(a)(1). Foreign person means someone other than the defined United States person, which includes U.S. citizens, lawful permanent residents, U.S.-organized entities and any person in the United States. The incorporated INA alien definition excludes U.S. citizens and nationals. Protected persons include any defined U.S. person unless the United States both formally consents to ICC jurisdiction and is a Rome Statute party. They also include foreign citizens or lawful residents of a NATO or designated major non-NATO ally that has not consented to ICC jurisdiction or is not a Rome Statute party. The listed military/government personnel are inclusive examples, not the entire protected class. The President may waive sanctions case by case for periods no longer than 90 days each on a reported vital-national-security determination before the waiver takes effect, including the specified detailed rationale and actions by the United States and ICC. The President may terminate sanctions on written certification that the ICC has ceased all covered efforts and permanently closed/withdrawn/ended/terminated them. Imposition also requires congressional briefing/written notice within 10 days. The package includes property blocking under existing IEEPA authorities and penalties, rescission of available ICC appropriations at enactment and a prospective ban on using appropriated funds for the ICC. Immigration membership follows the direct travel/admission/parole/benefit restrictions, not the foreign-affairs findings. These are proposed legislative requirements; existing general INA inadmissibility/temporary-admission authorities are not treated as newly created by this bill. Actual designation, visa revocation, sanctions, enforcement or enactment is not inferred.

Immigration sanctions extend to relatives who meet the INA alien definition; the principal-target foreign-person limitation is not assumed to exclude every lawful-permanent-resident relative. actions.candidate_exact_action_meaning: The exact House-passed H.R.30 adds INA 212(a)(2)(J) inadmissibility for a person convicted of, admitting commission of, or admitting acts constituting the essential elements of a sex offense under 34 USC 20911(5), or a conspiracy to commit one. New 212(a)(2)(K) uses those same conviction/admission predicates for a crime of domestic violence (defined through 237(a)(2)(E)), stalking, child abuse/neglect/abandonment, or a crime violating the protective-order portion addressing credible threats, repeated harassment or bodily injury. The INA baseline makes these inadmissibility grounds relevant to visas and admission; the bill is not limited by its title to persons unlawfully present. It separately adds INA 237(a)(2)(G) deportability for conviction of a defined sex offense or conspiracy: admission of conduct alone is not the predicate in this new deportability clause. The existing 237(a)(2)(E)(i) after-admission conviction ground for domestic violence, stalking and child abuse/neglect/abandonment remains; its domestic-violence definition is expanded to include any crime constituting domestic violence under 34 USC 12291(a), regardless of whether the jurisdiction receives grants. Noncriminal behavior mentioned in the victim-services portion of that definition is not itself converted into a crime by this bill. The incorporated sex-offense definition covers criminal sexual-act/contact offenses, specified offenses against minors, listed federal/military offenses, and attempts/conspiracies, with its foreign-conviction fairness and consensual-conduct limitations. The latter exclude specified consensual adult conduct unless custodial authority exists, and specified conduct where the victim is at least 13 and the offender is not more than 4 years older. Some covered conduct already can trigger existing criminal inadmissibility or deportability grounds; these are additional grounds and a definition expansion, not the creation of all immigration consequences for these crimes. INA 101(a)(48) supplies the existing conviction framework, including specified withheld adjudications with a guilt/plea/facts predicate plus court-ordered punishment, penalty or restraint. H.R.30 references 20911(5), rather than expressly importing the separate 20911(8) juvenile-conviction definition. The bill leaves the 237(a)(7) discretionary battered-person waiver for specified domestic-violence/stalking/protective-order deportability grounds intact; that waiver is not written to cover the new sex-offense ground. Existing 212(d)(3) discretionary temporary nonimmigrant admission and 212(d)(13)/(14) T/U status waiver authorities remain within their own conditions. Existing 212(h) enumerates other criminal grounds and is not expanded to the newJ/K grounds. No universal waiver or automatic removal is established.
actions.candidate_short_description: H.R.30 sex-offense and domestic-violence immigration grounds
actions.candidate_compact_description: H.R.30 would add sex-offense and specified domestic-violence-related inadmissibility grounds, add conviction-based sex-offense deportability, and broaden the existing domestic-violence deportability definition.
candidate_shared_limitations: The new inadmissibility clauses permit conviction or specified admissions. The new sex-offense deportability clause requires conviction. The existing domestic-violence/stalking/child-crime deportability clause retains its after-admission conviction condition; the existing protective-order clause separately depends on a court determination.

Sex-offense scope preserves 20911(5) foreign-conviction safeguards and consensual-conduct exclusions, including the at-least 13/not-more-than 4 years-older condition. The separate 20911(8) juvenile definition is not automatically treated as incorporated by the reference to(5); no individual juvenile-case conclusion is made.

The additional domestic-violence definition still requires a crime. Victim-service definitions that also describe noncriminal coercive conduct do not alone satisfy that predicate. Grant receipt is expressly irrelevant to the added definition.

The existing 237(a)(7) waiver requires a battered/extreme-cruelty victim who was not the primary perpetrator, and specified self-defense/protective-order/connected-crime conditions; the connected-crime route excludes serious bodily injury. The Attorney General retains credible-evidence discretion. This limited waiver does not extend automatically to new 237(a)(2)(G).

Existing inadmissibility exceptions and waivers retain their own enumerated scope. The 212(a)(2)(A) single-offense minor/petty-offense exceptions and 212(h) waiver are not stated as exceptions to newJ/K; retained 212(d)(3),T andU routes are discretionary and conditioned, rather than categorical relief.

This whole-bill House passage choice does not establish separate component preferences, wrongdoing, actual visa refusal, admission denial, deportation or enactment. The bill text addresses any alien meeting the grounds, rather than only unlawful presence suggested by its short title.

actions.mechanism: S.5: expanding specified immigration detention and State enforcement litigation
actions.candidate_exact_action_meaning: S.5 would extend the federal mandatory-custody category to the following offenses: burglary, theft, larceny, shoplifting, assault of a law-enforcement officer, or any crime resulting in another person's death or serious bodily injury. The listed property-offense terms, assault of a law-enforcement officer and serious bodily injury take the meanings assigned by the jurisdiction where the acts occurred. The exact bill adds an INA 236(c) mandatory-custody category requiring inadmissibility under INA 212(a)(6)(A), (6)(C), or (7) together with a specified criminal predicate: being charged, arrested, convicted, admitting commission, or admitting acts constituting the essential elements. These inadmissibility categories concern presence without admission/parole or undesignated arrival, material immigration fraud/false citizenship claims, and specified entry-document defects, subject to their existing statutory qualifications. DHS must issue a detainer for a person meeting the new ground and, if the person is not otherwise detained by Federal, State or local officials, effectively and expeditiously take custody. The bill also gives a State attorney general or other authorized State officer standing, on alleged harm to the State or residents (including financial harm in excess of $100), to seek appropriate injunctive relief in district court over five specified federal matters: INA 235(b)(1)/(2) detention/removal requirements; INA 236 release, bond or parole decisions; the existing INA 243(d) visa-discontinuance requirement for countries denying or unreasonably delaying acceptance; violation of the existing INA 212(d)(5)(A) case-by-case urgent-humanitarian/significant-public-benefit parole limits; and INA 241(a)(2) detention during the removal period. Courts must advance and expedite these cases to the greatest practicable extent. INA 236(e) removes its express release/grant shield while leaving the other printed discretionary-judgment/detention/revocation/denial restrictions, and INA 242(f)(1) receives an exception for the printed listed actions, while its separate final-removal-order injunction standard remains. These review changes do not establish a general right to enjoin every immigration action. The parole clause changes its named administering actor to the Secretary of Homeland Security. The baseline removal period is generally 90 days with specified starting/extension conditions; the bill adds litigation standing over its detention requirement rather than creating that period. The pre-existing narrow witness/cooperator-protection release exception remains, redesignated as INA 236(c)(4).
actions.candidate_short_description: S.5: expanding specified immigration detention and State enforcement litigation
actions.candidate_compact_description: S.5 would expand mandatory immigration custody and DHS detainers for the specified inadmissibility/offense combination (burglary, theft, larceny, shoplifting, assault of a law-enforcement officer, or any crime resulting in another person's death or serious bodily injury), and add harm-conditioned State suits over specified detention, release, parole and visa duties.
candidate_shared_limitations: The listed property-offense terms, assault of a law-enforcement officer and serious bodily injury take the meanings assigned by the jurisdiction where the acts occurred.

The new custody ground requires both inadmissibility under INA 212(a)(6)(A), (6)(C), or (7) and a listed offense predicate. Arrest or charge can suffice for the offense predicate; conviction is not required. Existing inadmissibility exceptions and waiver routes are not repealed, including specified battered-person/false-citizenship exceptions and document/fraud waivers.

The pre-existing INA 236(c) witness/cooperator-protection release exception is redesignated rather than repealed: release requires the specified protection necessity, no danger and likely appearance. Ordinary bond or parole is not substituted for that narrow exception.

State litigation requires alleged harm to the State or residents, including financial harm in excess of $100. Relief is appropriate injunctive relief and expedited handling to the greatest practicable extent; a filed suit or favorable judgment is not inferred.

Case-by-case humanitarian/significant-public-benefit parole limits and the conditional visa-discontinuance duty for countries refusing or delaying acceptance already exist. The bill adds State enforcement standing and related review changes; it does not newly create those substantive baseline limits.

The visa-discontinuance duty arises after the statutory federal notification that a foreign country denies or unreasonably delays acceptance after a request. It covers immigrant visas, nonimmigrant visas, or both for the specified nationals/residents in that country, and lasts until the statutory acceptance notice. These conditions are retained, not newly imposed.

The existing INA 236(c)(1) when-released framework remains; the new DHS detainer clause separately requires expeditious custody when the person is not otherwise detained. No actual detention timing or individual outcome is inferred.

This is a whole-bill House passage choice. It does not establish separate component positions, guilt, actual detention/removal, a successful suit or enactment. The parallel House and Senate bills remain distinct proposal episodes; later enacted text does not replace either exact voting version.

Apprehension and detention of aliens (a) Arrest, detention, and release On a warrant issued by the Attorney General, an alien may be arrested and detained pending a decision on whether the alien is to be removed from the United States. Except as provided in subsection (c) and pending such decision, the Attorney General— (1) may continue to detain the arrested alien; and (2) may release the alien on— (A) bond of at least $1,500 with security approved by, and containing conditions prescribed by, the Attorney General; or (B) conditional parole; but (3) may not provide the alien with work authorization (including an "employment authorized" endorsement or other appropriate work permit), unless the alien is lawfully admitted for permanent residence or otherwise would (without regard to removal proceedings) be provided such authorization. (b) Revocation of bond or parole The Attorney General at any time may revoke a bond or parole authorized under subsection (a), rearrest the alien under the original warrant, and detain the alien. (c) Detention of criminal aliens (1) Custody The Attorney General shall take into custody any alien who— (A) is inadmissible by reason of having committed any offense covered in section 1182(a)(2) of this title, (B) is deportable by reason of having committed any offense covered in section 1227(a)(2)(A)(ii), (A)(iii), (B), (C), or (D) of this title, (C) is deportable under section 1227(a)(2)(A)(i) of this title on the basis of an offense for which the alien has been sentence 1 to a term of imprisonment of at least 1 year, or (D) is inadmissible under section 1182(a)(3)(B) of this title or deportable under section 1227(a)(4)(B) of this title, when the alien is released, without regard to whether the alien is released on parole, supervised release, or probation, and without regard to whether the alien may be arrested or imprisoned again for the same offense. (2) Release The Attorney General may release an alien described in paragraph (1) only if the Attorney General decides pursuant to section 3521 of title 18 that release of the alien from custody is necessary to provide protection to a witness, a potential witness, a person cooperating with an investigation into major criminal activity, or an immediate family member or close associate of a witness, potential witness, or person cooperating with such an investigation, and the alien satisfies the Attorney General that the alien will not pose a danger to the safety of other persons or of property and is likely to appear for any scheduled proceeding. A decision relating to such release shall take place in accordance with a procedure that considers the severity of the offense committed by the alien. (d) Identification of criminal aliens (1) The Attorney General shall devise and implement a system— (A) to make available, daily (on a 24-hour basis), to Federal, State, and local authorities the investigative resources of the Service to determine whether individuals arrested by such authorities for aggravated felonies are aliens; (B) to designate and train officers and employees of the Service to serve as a liaison to Federal, State, and local law enforcement and correctional agencies and courts with respect to the arrest, conviction, and release of any alien charged with an aggravated felony; and (C) which uses computer resources to maintain a current record of aliens who have been convicted of an aggravated felony, and indicates those who have been removed. (3) Upon the request of the governor or chief executive officer of any State, the Service shall provide assistance to State courts in the identification of aliens unlawfully present in the United States pending criminal prosecution. (e) Judicial review The Attorney General's discretionary judgment regarding the application of this section shall not be subject to review. No court may set aside any action or decision by the Attorney General under this section regarding the detention or release of any alien or the grant, revocation, or denial of bond or parole.

actions.mechanism: H.R.35 immigration consequences for specified border vehicle flight
actions.candidate_exact_action_meaning: The exact House-passed H.R.35 adds 18 USC 40B: operating a motor vehicle within 100 miles of the United States border while intentionally fleeing a pursuing U.S. Border Patrol agent acting under lawful authority, or a pursuing Federal/State/local officer actively assisting or under Border Patrol command. The ordinary penalty alternatives are imprisonment up to 2 years, a title 18 fine, or both; where serious bodily injury results the imprisonment alternative is 5–20 years, and where any person's death results it is 10 years to life, with fine-or-both alternatives retained in both cases. The bill adds INA 212(a)(2)(J) inadmissibility and 237(a)(2)(G) deportability for any alien convicted of, admitting commission of, or admitting acts constituting the essential elements of 40B(a). It also inserts 208A making a person meeting that same predicate ineligible for relief under the immigration laws, expressly including asylum under 208. Neither arrest alone nor merely being within 100 miles is the printed immigration predicate. Pre-existing 18 USC 758 already criminalizes vehicle flight/evasion from an immigration or other federal checkpoint followed by fleeing law-enforcement agents above the legal speed limit, with up-to 5 years/fine/both; existing 237(a)(2)(A)(iv) already makes a conviction for 758 deportable. H.R.35 creates a different officer/geography/intent predicate and additional immigration consequences, rather than the first-ever immigration checkpoint-flight offense or deportability ground. Unlike that existing deportability ground, the newG also accepts specified admissions. Existing INA 101(a)(48) conviction rules remain. The Attorney General, with the Secretary of Homeland Security, must report annually to both Judiciary Committees on violations, charged/apprehended/not-charged/not-apprehended counts, and penalties sought/imposed. A reporting duty is not evidence of actual violations, convictions or enforcement. The separate broad relief-bar clause is preserved as printed; it is not replaced by a blanket claim that existing narrow waivers guarantee relief, and no individual asylum or removal outcome is decided.

actions.candidate_exact_action_meaning: The exact H.R.2056 EH proposal prohibits the District of Columbia from having a statute, ordinance, policy or practice that prohibits or restricts a District government entity or official from sending, receiving, maintaining or exchanging information about any individual's citizenship or immigration status, lawful or unlawful, with any Federal, State or local government entity. It separately prohibits such District restrictions on compliance with a lawfully made DHS request under INA 236 or 287 to comply with a detainer for, or notify about release of, an individual. This is an express D.C.-specific restriction on governmental policies/practices. Existing 8 USC 1373 and 1644 already contain statutory restrictions on limiting certain status-information exchanges with the immigration service; the bill is not the first general permission to communicate immigration status. The bill's printed information clause includes citizenship as well as status and communication with any listed governmental entity, while its separate lawful-request clause specifically addresses detainers/release notices. INA 236 and 287 already govern qualified immigration custody and officer powers, including specified custody/release conditions, arrest limits and cooperation provisions. H.R.2056 does not itself rewrite those authorities, deem every DHS request lawful, or establish that every individual detainer must be obeyed. It bars District policies restricting the specified lawful-request compliance; individual custody legality, actual information disclosure/detention/removal, implementation and enactment are not inferred.

actions.candidate_exact_action_meaning: The exact H.R.875 EH proposal adds INA 212(a)(2)(J) inadmissibility for any alien convicted of, admitting commission of, or admitting acts constituting the essential elements of an intoxicated/impaired-driving offense. The terms take their meaning under the law of the jurisdiction where the conviction, offense or essential acts occurred, expressly including alcohol/drug influence or impairment, without regard to misdemeanor/felony classification under Federal, State, tribal or local law. Existing INA 212(a) makes inadmissibility relevant to visas and admission. It separately adds INA 237(a)(2)(G) deportability for conviction of a jurisdiction-defined intoxicated/impaired-driving offense, including alcohol/drug influence or impairment, regardless of the listed misdemeanor/felony classification. That clause uses the law where conviction occurred and does not make admission of conduct alone its predicate. Neither clause requires an injury/death or multiple offenses. The existing INA 101(a)(48) conviction framework remains, including specified withheld-adjudication situations with guilt/plea/facts and court-ordered punishment/penalty/restraint. These are additional categorical statutory grounds, rather than a claim that covered conduct previously could never trigger other criminal inadmissibility or deportability. Existing criminal INA grounds retain their own elements and exceptions. The single-offense minor/petty-offense exception in 212(a)(2)(A), the enumerated 212(h) waiver, and the 237(a)(2)(A)(vi) pardon exception are not printed exceptions to new J/G. Existing discretionary temporary-nonimmigrant/T/U inadmissibility waiver routes are retained within their own conditions; no categorical relief, guilt or automatic deportation is inferred. The bill concerns any alien meeting the grounds, not only a person unlawfully present.
actions.candidate_compact_description: H.R.875 would add jurisdiction-defined intoxicated/impaired-driving inadmissibility based on conviction or specified admissions, and deportability based on conviction, regardless of misdemeanor/felony classification.
candidate_shared_limitations: The new inadmissibility predicate is conviction or the specified admissions; the new deportability predicate requires conviction. Arrest alone is not either printed predicate, and admission of conduct alone does not establish new G deportability.

Offense meanings follow the specified jurisdiction. Alcohol and drug impairment are expressly included; misdemeanor/felony classification is not a threshold. Neither new clause adds an injury/death, repeat-offense, imprisonment-length or after-admission condition of its own.

Existing INA conviction rules and other criminal grounds remain. Their enumerated petty-offense, pardon or 212(h) exceptions are not automatically extended to these new grounds. Retained temporary-admission/T/U waiver authorities are conditioned and discretionary rather than universal relief.
This is whole-bill House passage. It does not establish separate component preferences, actual guilt, visa/admission denial, removal or enactment; no preferred alternative follows from opposition.

actions.candidate_exact_action_meaning: The exact H.R.3486 EH proposal raises the INA 275(a) subsequent improper-entry offense imprisonment maximum from 2 to 5 years; the existing first-offense 6-month maximum/fine-or-both and other 275 provisions remain. New 275(e) covers an alien who enters/attempts entry at an undesignated time/place, eludes immigration examination/inspection, or attempts/obtains entry through willfully false/misleading representation or concealment of a material fact, and thereafter is convicted of a crime punishable by more than one year. That conjunction carries mandatory imprisonment of at least 5 years up to life, with an optional title 18 fine. Mere unlawful presence, arrest or all first entries do not alone satisfy it. INA 276(a) continues to require prior denial of admission/exclusion/deportation/removal or departure while a removal-type order is outstanding, followed by entry/attempt or being found in the United States. It raises the general maximum from 2 to 10 years, with fine-or-both alternatives. It preserves advance express consent to reapply and the specified prior-denial/removal no-advance-consent exception, naming DHS rather than the Attorney General. Rewritten 276(b), except where new(c) applies, raises the maximum for pre-removal conviction of at least 3 drug/person misdemeanors from 10 to 15 years. It retains the specified INA 235(c)/TitleV exclusion/removal unauthorized reentry category's 10-year nonconcurrent prison term plus fine, and the qualified 241(a)(4)(B) early-removal reentry category's 10-year maximum/fine-or-both. It adds a category for at least 3 prior denials/exclusions/deportations/removals followed by entry/attempt/being found, with 10-year maximum/fine-or-both. New 276(c) overrides(a)/(b) penalties for a covered reentrant convicted before removal/departure of an aggravated felony, any crime classed as a felony by the relevant Federal/State/Tribal/local jurisdiction, or any crime punishable by more than one year: mandatory imprisonment of at least 10 years up to life, with an optional fine. This replaces the prior felony/aggravated-felony maximums rather than changing every felony into an INA aggravated felony. The existing INA aggravated-felony definition and its offense-specific/foreign-offense qualifications remain. Stipulated-removal agreements during or outside Federal/State criminal trials count as removal for(b)/(c). The existing remainder-of-unserved-sentence reentry provision is redesignated(d), with its removal cross-reference and administering actor updated. Existing collateral attack on the underlying order remains redesignated(e), requiring exhaustion of available administrative remedies, improper deprivation of judicial review and fundamental unfairness. These are legislative penalty/actor/cross-reference changes; individual guilt, validity of a removal order, sentence, actual enforcement or enactment is not inferred.

Aggravated felony uses the retained INA definition, including its separate offense thresholds and foreign-offense 15-year completion qualification; the bill also independently covers jurisdiction-defined felonies and crimes punishable by more than one year. actions.candidate_exact_action_meaning: The exact H.R.4638 EH proposal adds INA 212(a)(2)(J) inadmissibility and 237(a)(2)(G) deportability for an alien convicted of, admitting commission of, or admitting acts constituting the essential elements of an offense under 18 USC 1368. Both new clauses allow those specified admissions, despite the conviction-only phrasing in the bill title. Arrest alone is not the printed predicate. The incorporated 1368 offense already criminalizes willfully and maliciously harming a police animal, including attempts and conspiracies. Police animal means a dog or horse employed by a Federal agency in any branch primarily to aid criminal detection, law enforcement or apprehension. It is not every working animal or every State/local police animal, and the bill is not limited to CBP animals. The existing offense carries fine and up-to 1year imprisonment, with up-to 10 years for permanent disability/disfigurement, serious bodily injury or death; the immigration clauses do not add an injury/penalty-length threshold. The bill adds INA consequences to that existing crime, not a new animal-harm offense or a claim that all covered conduct previously had no immigration consequences. Existing INA conviction rules/other criminal grounds remain. Their enumerated petty-offense,212(h) and pardon exceptions are not written as exceptions to newJ/G; discretionary temporary-admission/T/U waiver authorities remain within their own scope. No blanket relief or automatic deportation is inferred.
actions.candidate_compact_description: H.R.4638 would add inadmissibility and deportability based on conviction or specified admissions of an 18 USC 1368 offense: willfully and maliciously harming, attempting or conspiring to harm a qualified federally employed police dog or horse.
candidate_shared_limitations: Both new INA grounds allow conviction or specified admissions; neither requires conviction exclusively or follows from arrest alone. The incorporated offense requires willful and malicious harm, attempt or conspiracy.

The animal is a federally employed dog or horse with the specified principal criminal/law-enforcement purpose, regardless of Federal branch. All animals, all State/local police animals and only-CBP animals are unsupported expansions/narrowings.

18 USC 1368 is pre-existing. Its aggravated-harm prison ceiling is not an eligibility threshold in these new INA clauses; existing INA exceptions/waivers keep their own scope rather than universally attaching to newJ/G.
This complete bill passage choice establishes no component preference, animal injury, guilt, visa/admission denial, removal or enactment.

actions.candidate_exact_action_meaning: The exact H.R.1689 EH proposal directs the Secretary of Homeland Security, notwithstanding any other law, to designate Haiti for temporary protected status until the date three months after January 20,2029—April 20,2029. It is a mandatory country-specific designation for that stated duration rather than a newly created TPS program or a direction to apply only ordinary discretionary six-to-eighteen-month designation periods. It does not state that Haiti has never before been designated or resolve litigation/agency decisions about earlier designations. The pre-existing 8 USC 1254a framework distinguishes designation of a country from granting TPS to an individual national (or stateless person last habitually resident there). Individual eligibility requires continuous U.S. physical presence since the effective date of the most recent designation, residence since the designated date, registration, applicable admissibility and absence of statutory bars, with stated brief/casual/innocent absence and emergency-trip qualifications. The bill does not supply individual presence/residence/registration dates or remove these requirements. Existing bars include a U.S.-committed felony or at least two misdemeanors and the incorporated persecution, particularly serious crime, serious nonpolitical foreign crime, security/terrorism and firm-resettlement grounds. Existing admissibility exceptions and individual humanitarian/family-unity/public-interest waivers retain their specified nonwaivable criminal/security boundaries. TPS may be withdrawn for ineligibility, disqualifying absence or registration failure without good cause. For a person granted TPS, the existing framework supplies protection from removal during the status period and employment authorization; it does not itself grant permanent residence or citizenship, guarantee all public benefits or authorize a person abroad to enter to apply. Its status-based detention protection, consent-based travel and adjustment-status provisions keep their own limits. This bill imposes the country-duration mandate, not individual awards or actual implementation, removals, benefit outcomes or enactment.

candidate_shared_limitations: The printed endpoint is three months after January 20,2029. The notwithstanding-law country-duration mandate is distinct from the ordinary discretionary country-designation/periodic-review framework; no earlier agency/litigation outcome is inferred.

Country designation is not automatic TPS for every Haitian person. Individual nationality/stateless-last-residence, continuous presence/residence, registration, admissibility and bar conditions remain, including the stated limited absence exceptions and waiver boundaries.

Criminal/asylum-related eligibility bars, withdrawal conditions and specified nonwaivable inadmissibility grounds remain. The bill does not establish individual waiver decisions or unspecified presence/registration dates.

TPS protection and work authorization are temporary and conditional. They are not permanent residence, citizenship, general admission from abroad or guaranteed public assistance; no actual individual status award or removal outcome follows from this vote.
This is whole-bill House passage of the fixed Haiti designation, not an individual immigration adjudication or enactment.

Notwithstanding any other provision of law, the Secretary of Homeland Security shall designate Haiti for temporary protected status until the date that is 3 months after January 20, 2029. claim_source_map.passage: (a) Granting of status (1) In general In the case of an alien who is a national of a foreign state designated under subsection (b) (or in the case of an alien having no nationality, is a person who last habitually resided in such designated state) and who meets the requirements of subsection (c), the Attorney General, in accordance with this section— (A) may grant the alien temporary protected status in the United States and shall not remove the alien from the United States during the period in which such status is in effect, and (B) shall authorize the alien to engage in employment in the United States and provide the alien with an "employment authorized" endorsement or other appropriate work permit. (2) Duration of work authorization Work authorization provided under this section shall be effective throughout the period the alien is in temporary protected status under this section. (3) Notice (A) Upon the granting of temporary protected status under this section, the Attorney General shall provide the alien with information concerning such status under this section. (B) If, at the time of initiation of a removal proceeding against an alien, the foreign state (of which the alien is a national) is designated under subsection (b), the Attorney General shall promptly notify the alien of the temporary protected status that may be available under this section. (C) If, at the time of designation of a foreign state under subsection (b), an alien (who is a national of such state) is in a removal proceeding under this subchapter, the Attorney General shall promptly notify the alien of the temporary protected status that may be available under this section. (D) Notices under this paragraph shall be provided in a form and language that the alien can understand. (4) Temporary treatment for eligible aliens (A) In the case of an alien who can establish a prima facie case of eligibility for benefits under paragraph (1), but for the fact that the period of registration under subsection (c)(1)(A)(iv) has not begun, until the alien has had a reasonable opportunity to register during the first 30 days of such period, the Attorney General shall provide for the benefits of paragraph (1). (B) In the case of an alien who establishes a prima facie case of eligibility for benefits under paragraph (1), until a final determination with respect to the alien's eligibility for such benefits under paragraph (1) has been made, the alien shall be provided such benefits. (5) Clarification Nothing in this section shall be construed as authorizing the Attorney General to deny temporary protected status to an alien based on the alien's immigration status or to require any alien, as a condition of being granted such status, either to relinquish nonimmigrant or other status the alien may have or to execute any waiver of other rights under this chapter. The granting of temporary protected status under this section shall not be considered to be inconsistent with the granting of nonimmigrant status under this chapter. (b) Designations (1) In general The Attorney General, after consultation with appropriate agencies of the Government, may designate any foreign state (or any part of such foreign state) under this subsection only if— (A) the Attorney General finds that there is an ongoing armed conflict within the state and, due to such conflict, requiring the return of aliens who are nationals of that state to that state (or to the part of the state) would pose a serious threat to their personal safety; (B) the Attorney General finds that— (i) there has been an earthquake, flood, drought, epidemic, or other environmental disaster in the state resulting in a substantial, but temporary, disruption of living conditions in the area affected, (ii) the foreign state is unable, temporarily, to handle adequately the return to the state of aliens who are nationals of the state, and (iii) the foreign state officially has requested designation under this subparagraph; or (C) the Attorney General finds that there exist extraordinary and temporary conditions in the foreign state that prevent aliens who are nationals of the state from returning to the state in safety, unless the Attorney General finds that permitting the aliens to remain temporarily in the United States is contrary to the national interest of the United States. A designation of a foreign state (or part of such foreign state) under this paragraph shall not become effective unless notice of the designation (including a statement of the findings under this paragraph and the effective date of the designation) is published in the Federal Register. In such notice, the Attorney General shall also state an estimate of the number of nationals of the foreign state designated who are (or within the effective period of the designation are likely to become) eligible for temporary protected status under this section and their immigration status in the United States. (2) Effective period of designation for foreign states The designation of a foreign state (or part of such foreign state) under paragraph (1) shall— (A) take effect upon the date of publication of the designation under such paragraph, or such later date as the Attorney General may specify in the notice published under such paragraph, and (B) shall remain in effect until the effective date of the termination of the designation under paragraph (3)(B). For purposes of this section, the initial period of designation of a foreign state (or part thereof) under paragraph (1) is the period, specified by the Attorney General, of not less than 6 months and not more than 18 months. (3) Periodic review, terminations, and extensions of designations (A) Periodic review At least 60 days before end of the initial period of designation, and any extended period of designation, of a foreign state (or part thereof) under this section the Attorney General, after consultation with appropriate agencies of the Government, shall review the conditions in the foreign state (or part of such foreign state) for which a designation is in effect under this subsection and shall determine whether the conditions for such designation under this subsection continue to be met. The Attorney General shall provide on a timely basis for the publication of notice of each such determination (including the basis for the determination, and, in the case of an affirmative determination, the period of extension of designation under subparagraph (C)) in the Federal Register. (B) Termination of designation If the Attorney General determines under subparagraph (A) that a foreign state (or part of such foreign state) no longer continues to meet the conditions for designation under paragraph (1), the Attorney General shall terminate the designation by pub lishing notice in the Federal Register of the determination under this subparagraph (including the basis for the determination). Such termination is effective in accordance with subsection (d)(3), but shall not be effective earlier than 60 days after the date the notice is published or, if later, the expiration of the most recent previous extension under subparagraph (C). (C) Extension of designation If the Attorney General does not determine under subparagraph (A) that a foreign state (or part of such foreign state) no longer meets the conditions for designation under paragraph (1), the period of designation of the foreign state is extended for an additional period of 6 months (or, in the discretion of the Attorney General, a period of 12 or 18 months). (4) Information concerning protected status at time of designations At the time of a designation of a foreign state under this subsection, the Attorney General shall make available information respecting the temporary protected status made available to aliens who are nationals of such designated foreign state. (5) Review (A) Designations There is no judicial review of any determination of the Attorney General with respect to the designation, or termination or extension of a designation, of a foreign state under this subsection. (B) Application to individuals The Attorney General shall establish an administrative procedure for the review of the denial of benefits to aliens under this subsection. Such procedure shall not prevent an alien from asserting protection under this section in removal proceedings if the alien demonstrates that the alien is a national of a state designated under paragraph (1). (c) Aliens eligible for temporary protected status (1) In general (A) Nationals of designated foreign states Subject to paragraph (3), an alien, who is a national of a state designated under subsection (b)(1) (or in the case of an alien having no nationality, is a person who last habitually resided in such designated state), meets the requirements of this paragraph only if— (i) the alien has been continuously physically present in the United States since the effective date of the most recent designation of that state; (ii) the alien has continuously resided in the United States since such date as the Attorney General may designate; (iii) the alien is admissible as an immigrant, except as otherwise provided under paragraph (2)(A), and is not ineligible for temporary protected status under paragraph (2)(B); and (iv) to the extent and in a manner which the Attorney General establishes, the alien registers for the temporary protected status under this section during a registration period of not less than 180 days. (B) Registration fee The Attorney General may require payment of a reasonable fee as a condition of registering an alien under subparagraph (A)(iv) (including providing an alien with an "employment authorized" endorsement or other appropriate work permit under this section). The amount of any such fee shall not exceed $50. In the case of aliens registered pursuant to a designation under this section made after July 17, 1991, the Attorney General may impose a separate, additional fee for providing an alien with documentation of work authorization. Notwithstanding section 3302 of title 31, all fees collected under this subparagraph shall be credited to the appropriation to be used in carrying out this section. (2) Eligibility standards (A) Waiver of certain grounds for inadmissibility In the determination of an alien's admissibility for purposes of subparagraph (A)(iii) of paragraph (1)— (i) the provisions of paragraphs (5) and (7)(A) of section 1182(a) of this title shall not apply; (ii) except as provided in clause (iii), the Attorney General may waive any other provision of section 1182(a) of this title in the case of individual aliens for humanitarian purposes, to assure family unity, or when it is otherwise in the public interest; but (iii) the Attorney General may not waive— (I) paragraphs (2)(A) and (2)(B) (relating to criminals) of such section, (II) paragraph (2)(C) of such section (relating to drug offenses), except for so much of such paragraph as relates to a single offense of simple possession of 30 grams or less of marijuana, or (III) paragraphs (3)(A), (3)(B), (3)(C), and (3)(E) of such section (relating to national security and participation in the Nazi persecutions or those who have engaged in genocide). (B) Aliens ineligible An alien shall not be eligible for temporary protected status under this section if the Attorney General finds that— (i) the alien has been convicted of any felony or 2 or more misdemeanors committed in the United States, or (ii) the alien is described in section 1158(b)(2)(A) of this title. (3) Withdrawal of temporary protected status The Attorney General shall withdraw temporary protected status granted to an alien under this section if— (A) the Attorney General finds that the alien was not in fact eligible for such status under this section, (B) except as provided in paragraph (4) and permitted in subsection (f)(3), the alien has not remained continuously physically present in the United States from the date the alien first was granted temporary protected status under this section, or (C) the alien fails, without good cause, to register with the Attorney General annually, at the end of each 12-month period after the granting of such status, in a form and manner specified by the Attorney General. (4) Treatment of brief, casual, and innocent departures and certain other absences (A) For purposes of paragraphs (1)(A)(i) and (3)(B), an alien shall not be considered to have failed to maintain continuous physical presence in the United States by virtue of brief, casual, and innocent absences from the United States, without regard to whether such absences were authorized by the Attorney General. (B) For purposes of paragraph (1)(A)(ii), an alien shall not be considered to have failed to maintain continuous residence in the United States by reason of a brief, casual, and innocent absence described in subparagraph (A) or due merely to a brief temporary trip abroad required by emergency or extenuating circumstances outside the control of the alien. (5) Construction Nothing in this section shall be construed as authorizing an alien to apply for admission to, or to be admitted to, the United States in order to apply for temporary protected status under this section. (6) Confidentiality of information The Attorney General shall establish procedures to protect the confidentiality of information provided by aliens under this section. (d) Documentation (1) Initial issuance Upon the granting of temporary protected status to an alien under this section, the Attorney General shall provide for the issuance of such temporary documentation and authorization as may be necessary to carry out the purposes of this section. (2) Period of validity Subject to paragraph (3), such documentation shall be valid during the initial period of designation of the foreign state (or part thereof) involved and any extension of such period. The Attorney General may stagger the periods of validity of the documentation and authorization in order to provide for an orderly renewal of such documentation and authorization and for an orderly transition (under paragraph (3)) upon the termination of a designation of a foreign state (or any part of such foreign state). (3) Effective date of terminations If the Attorney General terminates the designation of a foreign state (or part of such foreign state) under subsection (b)(3)(B), such termination shall only apply to documentation and authorization issued or renewed after the effective date of the publication of notice of the determination under that subsection (or, at the Attorney General's option, after such period after the effective date of the determination as the Attorney General determines to be appropriate in order to provide for an orderly transition). (4) Detention of alien An alien provided temporary protected status under this section shall not be detained by the Attorney General on the basis of the alien's immigration status in the United States. (e) Relation of period of temporary protected status to cancellation of removal With respect to an alien granted temporary protected status under this section, the period of such status shall not be counted as a period of physical presence in the United States for purposes of section 1229b(a) of this title, unless the Attorney General determines that extreme hardship exists. Such period shall not cause a break in the continuity of residence of the period before and after such period for purposes of such section. (f) Benefits and status during period of temporary protected status During a period in which an alien is granted temporary protected status under this section— (1) the alien shall not be considered to be permanently residing in the United States under color of law; (2) the alien may be deemed ineligible for public assistance by a State (as defined in section 1101(a)(36) of this title) or any political subdivision thereof which furnishes such assistance; (3) the alien may travel abroad with the prior consent of the Attorney General; and (4) for purposes of adjustment of status under section 1255 of this title and change of status under section 1258 of this title, the alien shall be considered as being in, and maintaining, lawful status as a nonimmigrant. (g) Exclusive remedy Except as otherwise specifically provided, this section shall constitute the exclusive authority of the Attorney General under law to permit aliens who are or may become otherwise deportable or have been paroled into the United States to remain in the United States temporarily because of their particular nationality or region of foreign state of nationality. (h) Limitation on consideration in Senate of legislation adjusting status (1) In general Except as provided in paragraph (2), it shall not be in order in the Senate to consider any bill, resolution, or amendment that— (A) provides for adjustment to lawful temporary or permanent resident alien status for any alien receiving temporary protected status under this section, or (B) has the effect of amending this subsection or limiting the application of this subsection. (2) Supermajority required Paragraph (1) may be waived or suspended in the Senate only by the affirmative vote of three-fifths of the Members duly chosen and sworn. An affirmative vote of three-fifths of the Members of the Senate duly chosen and sworn shall be required in the Senate to sustain an appeal of the ruling of the Chair on a point of order raised under paragraph (1). (3) Rules Paragraphs (1) and (2) are enacted— (A) as an exercise of the rulemaking power of the Senate and as such they are deemed a part of the rules of the Senate, but applicable only with respect to the matters described in paragraph (1) and supersede other rules of the Senate only to the extent that such paragraphs are inconsistent therewith; and (B) with full recognition of the constitutional right of the Senate to change such rules at any time, in the same manner as in the case of any other rule of the Senate. (i) Annual report and review (1) Annual report Not later than March 1 of each year (beginning with 1992), the Attorney General, after consultation with the appropriate agencies of the Government, shall submit a report to the Committees on the Judiciary of the House of Representatives and of the Senate on the operation of this section during the previous year. Each report shall include— (A) a listing of the foreign states or parts thereof designated under this section, (B) the number of nationals of each such state who have been granted temporary protected status under this section and their immigration status before being granted such status, and (C) an explanation of the reasons why foreign states or parts thereof were designated under subsection (b)(1) and, with respect to foreign states or parts thereof previously designated, why the designation was terminated or extended under subsection (b)(3). (2) Committee report No later than 180 days after the date of receipt of such a report, the Committee on the Judiciary of each House of Congress shall report to its respective House such oversight findings and legislation as it deems appropriate.

basis: The printed endpoint is three months after January 20,2029. The notwithstanding-law country-duration mandate is distinct from the ordinary discretionary country-designation/periodic-review framework; no earlier agency/litigation outcome is inferred.

Country designation is not automatic TPS for every Haitian person. Individual nationality/stateless-last-residence, continuous presence/residence, registration, admissibility and bar conditions remain, including the stated limited absence exceptions and waiver boundaries.

Criminal/asylum-related eligibility bars, withdrawal conditions and specified nonwaivable inadmissibility grounds remain. The bill does not establish individual waiver decisions or unspecified presence/registration dates.

TPS protection and work authorization are temporary and conditional. They are not permanent residence, citizenship, general admission from abroad or guaranteed public assistance; no actual individual status award or removal outcome follows from this vote.
This is whole-bill House passage of the fixed Haiti designation, not an individual immigration adjudication or enactment.
